dhq:abstract.p: Archivists, designers, and scholars speak a hybrid, ad-hoc language when they negotiate how collections should appear on-screen. This paper namesWords like ‘generous’ or ‘unfolding’ do work that emergent idiom neither computer science nor cultural theory does on their own, and usually vanish once the project ends. I call this a pidgin philosophy for data visualization and examinesexamine its methodological value. for research and design. div.head: Introduction
div.p: 28 August 2013. Ten people are cutting up photographs into collages at a table in the Architecture Building of Newcastle University in the UK. These images come from the Amber Film & Photography Collective’s archive of working-class life in North East England. Those taking part in the workshop titled 'Finding new Pathways in Rich Archives' include members of the collective, artists, and researchers . They barely share a vocabulary for what an archive interface should look like. During the discussion, one participant warns that if everybody can contribute, the story they are trying to open up may be lost. However, opening the archive is the point of the exercise, but opening it too far also poses a danger to this mission. The notion of ‘opening’ carries multiple meanings. For the curator the word signals access, for the designer an interface gesture, and for the researcher a claim about interpretation. Nobody stops to fix the ambiguity of the term, and the conversation proceeds. That is what this paper is about: words that coordinate work precisely because they have not been pinned down. ‘Opening’ holds the group’s competing commitments together long enough for the more difficult negotiations to take place over what to show and on whose terms.

The workshop in Newcastle held several incompatible answers to the question of how to open an archive, let alone what an archive actually is. Archives have never been neutral repositories of evidence. From their inception, they have been tangled in competing projects of power and preservation. Born alongside the modern nation-state, historical archives enshrined both official memory and governmental authority . Even in their earliest photographic manifestations, archives had a dual purpose: honorific when celebrating respected citizens, repressive when sorting bodies into criminological types . They can be viewed as both sites of authority and sets of archiving processes that actively shape what will count as memory . Likewise, the humanities tend to theorize the archive as a place of power and memory work, whereas archival studies aim to advance more practical frameworks for creating and maintaining archives . A central concern of archival work is provenance, which is not merely the point of origin of archival objects, but the network of relationships between objects, agents and functions . Archives are approached by many with a mix of positivist promise and voyeuristic desire, drawn by the allure of recovering a lost past while attempting the reanimation of ghostly traces on today’s terms .

Recent practices further expand the promise of the archive, from activist collections mobilizing documents as tools of empowerment () to digital editors seeking sensory pleasure in the flexible remediation of manuscript ecologies [Kim 2018]. Critical archivists call for a shift from rights-based neutrality toward radical empathy and liberatory memory work ; . Digitizing cultural heritage now places archives at a flashpoint: big-data surveillance and platform capitalism demand exposure and extraction at scale, while communities and scholars call for provenance and epistemic justice . Nowhere is this tension sharper than for materials of Indigenous origin. Many cultural collections were gathered through dispossession or coercion. Now, communities are demanding the return of these collections and for community-led governance that allows for culturally appropriate access . These contradictory custodial imperatives set the stage for difficult deliberations about the design of archive interfaces.

Under pressure to widen access and empower communities while protecting sensitive materials and resisting extraction and surveillance, mixed teams consisting of digital archivists, interface designers, and humanities scholars communicate about prototypes and platforms that attempt to reconcile these conflicting demands. During such exchanges, the conversation slips into a hybrid language. Database ‘records’ mingle with discussions of ‘provenance’; ‘users’ become ‘visitors’; and the viability of a prototype is judged by the likelihood of ‘serendipity’. This improvised idiom is neither the technical jargon of computer science nor the theoretical argot of cultural studies; it is a vocabulary in-between, assembled on the fly so that disparate expertise can hold a collaborative project together and pursue ambitions at the crossroads. This language gives teams a way to deliberate how and when cultural materials should be displayed or withheld, rather than assuming access as a given. Following the idea of disciplinary trading zones (), this paper recognizes this hybrid language as an emergent pidgin philosophy for the visualization of cultural collections.

Visualization’s own long history foreshadows this linguistic bricolage. Long before screens or algorithms, people marked walls and knotted cords to translate experience into a compressed form, from the Altamira bison drawings to the Andean quipus ; . Modernity overlaid statistical reasoning on that heritage: from William Playfair’s charts of international trade to Florence Nightingale’s diagrams of preventable death in army hospitals . W.E.B. Du Bois created information graphics representing African Americans’ social conditions at the turn of the 20th century (), and a few years later Otto and Marie Neurath, along with Gerd Arntz, developed a visualization system to convey the complexity of social change in Austria . John Tukey’s exploratory data analysis showed that algorithms could accelerate what pencils once attempted, inviting ever-larger datasets onto the screen . Over the last two decades, digital humanities projects have re-appropriated these methods, for example, to map colonial slave trade (), reveal literary correspondence networks (), represent the sonic patterns of poetry (), or, more generally, open up exploratory access to cultural collections . The growing use of visualization in the humanities has already prompted a reconsideration of the vocabulary for interpretative practices .

What is missing is neither theory nor technique, both of which are plentiful, but a working vocabulary that survives the time frame of a particular project. This paper therefore shifts from devising new visualization techniques to doing vocabulary work: reclaiming words that could keep collection interfaces open to surprise, friction, and care. It gathers three terms—wanderer, fold, and shimmer—that are starting to circulate in interdisciplinary conversations. Unpacking each term through feminist () and pluriversal () lenses makes visible the commitments already implicit in contemporary data work and design practice. Naming those commitments as a pidgin philosophy is meant to embed them in the active vocabulary of interdisciplinary research and design. The terms can be understood as ‘strong concepts’ ), intermediate-level knowledge that travels between specific designs. Crucially, noticing a pidgin should not fossilize it: by definition it remains open-ended, patched together from languages at hand, and remade with every new encounter . The lexicon presented here is offered in the spirit of a conceptual commons open to revision, not a fixed inventory. It matters what stories make worlds, what worlds make stories (), and vocabulary work is one way of remaining open for more stories than one.

In this paper, I attempt three things: 1) trace the pidgin philosophy’s emergence and justify vocabulary work as a methodological stance, 2) describe three terms through their lineages, theoretical commitments, and practical examples, and 3) synthesize them into a cross-cutting grammar for the design and study of collection visualizations. But before proceeding, a word on where this comes from. This is an interpretive account rather than an ethnography: in addition to readings of scholarly publications, the observations about how mixed teams talk come from co-design projects since 2013, beginning with the Newcastle workshop () and continuing in numerous projects in Potsdam (e.g., ). For this article, I coded no transcripts and counted no term frequencies. The interfaces discussed below I consider as texts to be interpreted. However, I was involved in the creation of several of them. The paper is addressed to the people who make such interfaces and to those who study them.

Following Caswell’s distinction between ‘the archive’ of humanities theory and ‘an archives’ with provenance and a custodian (), I write ‘collection’ for any body of digitized cultural material and reserve ‘archive’ for cases where provenance, custodianship, or terms of access are critical. Most of the interfaces discussed in this paper are in fact museum and library projects rather than archival ones.

div.head: Pidgin Philosophy as a Living Lexicon
div.p:
In historical linguistics a pidgin is a pragmatic contact language that emerges when communities without a shared language need to trade, build, or govern together . Its vocabulary is blended and its grammar is minimal—just enough words and phrases to load the ships and sign the treaty. Pidgins also arise in situ between domains, exemplifying what science studies scholars may call a trading zone idiom (): a stripped down but creative language that lets specialists cooperate without fully understanding one another’s disciplinary terms. Visualization projects that straddle archival studies, interface design, and digital humanities show similar dynamics, when an archivist explains a finding aid convention to a visualization researcher or when a literary scholar sketches an interface idea for a designer. Fragments of archive theory, cultural studies, visual analytics, and other disciplines fuse into sentences that belong fully to none of the contributing fields. During co-creation workshops and feedback sessions, phrases like ‘serendipitous encounters’ [Foster and Ford 2003], ‘generous interfaces’ (), ‘unfolding details’ (), or ‘critical cognition’ () seem to appear out of nowhere.
They prove useful, but then often vanish once the prototypes are launched and the papers are published. The notion of ‘sandcastling’ names the ephemeral visualizations that mediate between disciplines, giving a team a word for the design process itself . Recognizing such fleeting speech as a pidgin helps us appreciate its performative power despite its ephemeral nature. ‘Performative’ here refers to how language can actively shape social connections and make commitments, which aligns with speech act theory and a more general performative turn in cultural studies . It is also evident in many Indigenous knowledge practices, where speaking is a means of establishing relations and responsibilities . Considering this hybrid speech a pidgin philosophy foregrounds its pragmatic character and shared ethos that lets collaborative work proceed before perfect translations are found.

A related concept to this pidgin philosophy is that of boundary objects, initially developed by Susan Leigh Star and James R. Griesemer in their seminal study of a natural history museum . They found that cooperation among amateur collectors, academic biologists, and museum administrators was made possible through objects such as specimens and maps. These items carried different meanings for each group yet provided enough common structure for coordinated work, bridging social worlds while accommodating divergent interests. Boundary objects have since been used to understand collaboration across institutions and worldviews, including classification systems in queer archives () and interdisciplinary knowledge integration . In a similar vein, visualization artifacts produced during design study processes can themselves function as boundary objects that support sense-making and decision-making across stakeholder groups in heterogeneous organizational contexts . In contrast to boundary objects that center artifacts, I want to foreground language itself as the medium of negotiation, focusing on terms that carry just enough resonance across disciplines to support mutual orientation. For example, ‘generosity’ and ‘serendipity’ do not function as shared artifacts, but rather as discursive bridges. While boundary objects enable work despite divergent views, a pidgin philosophy can synthesize diverse perspectives into a shared vocabulary with which to develop a collective vision.

Pidgin words can be powerful during the time frame of a project, but they can evaporate once the team disbands, forcing the next collaboration to reinvent its vocabulary from scratch. Amber is my exemplar here . By the end of that afternoon a group of artists, archive members, and researchers had arrived at a shared way of describing the collection as a living archive that grows and changes over time and its exploration akin to walking as an open-ended mode of engagement. None of us could have done that in the morning.
However, that shared idiom did not outlive the day. Fragments of it may have travelled on in individual speakers, but as a common language it dissolved when the group did. Rather than standardizing and preserving the language (which would diminish its agility), I propose a limited lexicon as a small starting point, or rather waypoint, for terminological reflection at the intersection of archives, design, and humanities.
Debates inside humanist visualization have already revolved around naming. When Johanna Drucker argues that scholars should treat data as ‘capta’—that is, taken, not given—she is not suggesting a new chart type but a new word to reorient research and design values . Mitchell Whitelaw’s call for ‘generous interfaces’ likewise substitutes a normative adjective for the default of efficient search in cultural collections . Feminist data visualization asks designers to consider categories to be contingent, to embrace affective and embodied experiences, and to examine power relations within project teams . Across these interventions, terminology operates as a catalyst for design and critique in heterogeneous groups. The pidgin philosophy is intended to equip interdisciplinary teams with a living lexicon to articulate what ‘good’ visualization practices might look like when aesthetics and ethics meet.

The sections that follow discuss three terms—wanderer, fold, and shimmer—that encapsulate ideas already being exchanged in the trading zone of archive studies, interface design, and digital humanities. Clearly, three terms do not make a lexicon, but they serve as seeds for a grammar of design principles and research methods. I selected these terms because they respond to critical commitments in cultural heritage: relations over objects, duration over speed, and gaps over totality. However, someone else at this interdisciplinary crossroads would probably have picked others.

div.head: Wanderer
div.p: The figure of the wanderer offers a counterimage to the rational and rushed ‘user’ at the center of most information-seeking models. Whereas a conventional searcher quickly scans a result list for relevant sources, the wanderer enters an information landscape willing to pause and ready to be surprised. This disposition fosters a kind of care for overlooked materials, for the invisible labor of collection-making, and for the stories that connect different archival worlds.

div.head: Origins
div.p: The notion of a calm and curious wanderer originates in the nineteenth-century flâneur strolling the streets of Paris (; ), but should be broadened here to include wayfarers () and the flaneuse . Prior work draws from the historical figure of the flâneur to formulate design cues for digital interfaces: just as the urban stroller drifts between arcades and alleyways, an information flaneur moves from item to item, noticing beauty and contradiction along the way . Echoing the qualities of exploratory search () and leisurely browsing ), the information flaneur engages in open-ended and casual information seeking. This poetic persona is a deliberate rejection of deficiency-based conceptions of information seekers, replacing the anxious searcher with an attentive wanderer .

While the digital environments may appear disembodied, the politics of movement still shape who feels safe and welcome to explore at leisure. The flâneur’s freedom to look and linger depended on a range of social and economic privileges. Susan Buck-Morss complicates idealized notions of the flâneur and places him on a continuum with the street’s less celebrated, more marginalized figures . In her reading, flânerie is possible only within a political economy that turns idleness into both commodity and threat. The gaze that lingers in front of shop windows is never far from the policing of loitering. Elizabeth Wilson presses the question further, arguing that the flâneur is less a figure of mastery than of unease, and that the city has been for women both a site of danger and one of unexpected freedom . Even so, the freedom to linger has never been evenly distributed. Simone Browne shows how racialized surveillance renders unhurried movement suspect, while the same slowness is read as leisure when practiced by white pedestrians . These dynamics carry over to digital space, where freedom to wander is constrained by bandwidth, language, censorship, and tracking systems. Wandering in an archive unfolds both within and in tension with its rules of gathering and organizing contents and the terms of entry . Rather than claiming frictionless access, wanderer-aware interfaces could make thresholds legible: who is hosted, under what authority, and which traces are retained.

To challenge the androcentric and Eurocentric pedigree of the flaneur, two complementary threads can be woven into the wanderer. First, feminist flânerie foregrounds safety, self-definition, and resistance against surveillance . Collection interfaces should expose positionality cues and allow annotation layers where marginalized wanderers can leave counternarratives. Second, Indigenous wayfaring reframes movement as relation-making . Inuit conceptions of travel characterize wayfaring as a way of being, in which the traveler quite literally becomes the line of travel, sustaining identity through an unfolding mesh of paths that link people, animals, and land as co-participants rather than as origins and destinations. A wanderer-aware interface can echo this by making relations visible: how a photograph is tied to land, kin, or species, and where those threads lead if followed laterally rather than down a hierarchy. Together these perspectives shift wandering from idle luxury to an ethic of attentive movement: traversing digital environments slowly enough to perceive what is usually overlooked.

div.head: Meanings
div.p: To embrace the ethos of the wanderer during design, navigating the collection as a kind of wandering can be translated into three commitments for digital interfaces.

Mindful meandering. Interfaces that serve wanderers should let curiosity, not efficiency, dictate movement. Instead of channeling visitors through a search box toward a ranked list, a wander-aware design offers multiple thresholds and represents progress as a branching constellation. Visual cues can hint at untaken side streets, encouraging the wanderer to drift laterally and discover the collection’s breadth before diving into depth. This resembles the common experience in a physical reading room, where the careful handling of boxes and files often leads to slow discovery. Yet in digital settings, slow looking often registers as inactivity in analytics dashboards, even though it is central to the ethos of wandering. The importance of slowness is also echoed in Indigenous pedagogies, where slow reflection is essential to learning and being in the world . Designers can affirm the value of slow perusal by disabling aggressive session time-outs, preserving navigation histories, and displaying subtle hints affirming that browsing without hurry is welcome.

Relational revelation. A wanderer’s detours are most rewarding when they expose hidden ties. Whenever an item comes into view, the interface should foreground its web of relationships among linked people, places, events, and subjects. By letting wanderers move across relational views, the interface honors the collection’s layered structure and helps visitors sense how any single record participates in larger, intertwined stories. This vision aligns with long-standing efforts in the heritage community to model complex connections among records, actors, and contexts. Notably, Records in Contexts by the International Council on Archives provides a framework of entities and relations for archival description . Similarly, CIDOC-CRM provides a general ontology for expressing event- and object-based connections across archives, libraries, and museums . When a visualization exposes these links, metadata ceases to be back-room matter and becomes part of exploratory travel.

Reflexive gaze. Looking is never neutral. Who we are shapes what we see, and archives are thick with symbols of power. Interfaces could surface this situatedness through lightweight changes to wording, letting wanderers reflect on their own position in relation to the archive. Role badges such as ‘public passerby,’ ‘contributing member,’ or ‘registered researcher’ could appear in the header, reminding every wanderer that the view is partial and shaped by standpoint. Such framing would ideally be developed with the communities whose materials are held, so that the roles reflect lived relationships to the archive. Infrastructural aspects such as scanner settings, digitization credits, and redaction notices might hover at the margins, pointing to the labor, privilege, or censorship beneath each record. Furthermore, a clickstream layer could let visitors inspect their own paths, asking whether they have drifted into confirmation loops or entered unfamiliar ground. Such devices could turn wandering from pleasant drift into a reflexive practice: an oscillation between recognizing the archive’s street signs of authority and acknowledging one’s own position therein.
These commitments shift the design question from How do we guide users to items quickly? to How do we host wanderers so they can linger, wonder, and connect within and across archival worlds?

Because wandering privileges open-ended movement, it can clash with institutional requirements for preservation, copyright, or cultural protocol. Designers must therefore negotiate between openness and sovereignty. For Indigenous archives, wanderer-centered interfaces should default to invitation-based rather than unrestricted download. In addition, for sensitive community collections, wandering could be staged through curated pathways coauthored with stakeholders. Accessibility is another stake: exploratory navigation must be viable via screen reader and on low-bandwidth connections. Providing alternative text for visual material and offering lightweight webpages can help make sure that wandering is not reserved for the fully sighted or broadband-privileged.

div.head: Usage
div.p: The ethos of the wanderer is already partially realized in interaction techniques of experimental collection interfaces. In the following, three examples demonstrate the practical viability of wandering as an alternative mode of access and appreciation.

Collections Dive was created for Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums as a probe into tempo-based browsing . Visitors enter a generous grid of thumbnail tiles that stretches far beyond the viewport and is replenished continuously when scrolling down. The engine samples the aggregated corpus according to scroll speed: slow scrolling returns similar objects, fast scrolling retrieves artifacts from distant domains. Every click shows more detail on a given item, and the items a visitor selects generate a retrospective network map that weaves them into a web of shared keywords. Coupling tempo-sensitive drift with a reflective navigation network, this playful interaction demonstrates how a collection interface could cultivate attentiveness, surface latent relationships without hierarchy, and invite reflection on the path that led there.

Dive into Color takes a different route, using perceptual hue as the organizing logic for artifacts drawn from Cooper Hewitt’s design holdings. After selecting a segment in a color wheel, matching catalog records are rendered as tiles placed along a temporal layout. Because hue rarely maps neatly onto curatorial taxonomies, browsing becomes an act of lateral association: a vase with blue décor may nudge up against a blue soup spoon. Curators testing the interface report that the layout can trigger questions about gaps in metadata, as when a hue selection generates an oddly sparse timeline. A side drawer tracks every tile the viewer hovers over, allowing chromatic detours to be retraced. The color field promotes open-ended drift, while the chromatic adjacency of items foregrounds material and historical links that standard searches tend to miss.

figure.head: Relational Perspectives for the Raoul Hausmann collection, here centered on ‘Der Dada’ (1919): every available attribute of the item opens its own column of related artifacts, offering as many lateral jumps as the item has facets. Later items appear above the selection and earlier ones below, so that scrolling up or down moves forward or backward in time .

div.p: Where the previous two projects privilege an open drift, the Relational Perspectives interface for the Raoul Hausmann collection invites visitors to pivot the corpus from successive item-based vantage points . The entry mosaic presents a faceted overview, but once an artifact is chosen, it is placed in the middle of the interface in the context of related items (see Figure 1). Each click on another artifact re-centers the display on the new focal item, enabling lateral hops among photographs, collages, and letters, producing an almost kaleidoscopic form of navigation. The temporal view makes indeterminacies more explicit, with gradient bands stretching across spans where dates are ambiguous, surfacing the gaps in collection knowledge.

Against the three commitments these examples are uneven. All three interfaces support mindful meandering, and two support relational revelation (Collections Dive and Relational Perspectives). Reflexive gaze is absent from all three, since none tells a visitor who they are taken to be or what is being logged about them. Wandering as movement is well developed. However, wandering as a situated and observed act is not (yet) well supported.

div.head: Fold
div.p: Having followed the wanderer along the archive’s shelves and boxes, we now consider the fabric of those structures themselves. If the wanderer foregrounds attentive movement, the fold orients us to the form of the interface: the mutable contours that appear and contract as we drag, scroll, and click. Just as a traveler rolls and unrolls a map to reveal new routes without tearing the paper, a folding interface must expand detail while preserving the context of the whole.

div.head: Origins
div.p: The fold enters contemporary theory through Gilles Deleuze’s reading of Leibniz, where every phenomenon is figured as a pleated surface whose successive explications, implications, and complications knit thought to matter . In visualization research the metaphor has been adopted to describe zooms, semantic lenses, and other interactions that reveal fine detail without disrupting the larger context . Deleuze’s baroque lineage, however, is only one thread.

Many Indigenous knowledge systems understand folding and weaving not as metaphors but as ontological practices that make the world. In Mesoamerica, the topology of the cosmos is conceived as a fabric whose solar obverse and intensive reverse are separated, and so brought into being, by an incessant operation of folding, the movement by which fragments of the other side fold themselves into the solar world and solar beings unfold back into the virtual domain . Textile arts supply the conceptual template for this cosmology: ritual bundles and body wrappings are understood as folds that momentarily stabilize a heterogeneous multiplicity before it slips away again. Here, to fold is already to relate, and every crease is an event of passage and transformation. A comparable logic is articulated in Warlpiri and Yolŋu thought.
In dialogue with Samuel Curkpatrick, the senior Warlpiri elder and scholar Wanta Jampijinpa Pawu describes ngurra-kurlu (home-having) as a pattern for living handed down from the ancestors, one that shows how everything is related. It has many names, one of them sacred and spoken only by men in initiation ceremony. That name has to do with weaving and is also a name for the Southern Cross, whose stars weave together into the diamond shape representing the whole of ngurra-kurlu. As Pawu puts it, it is not you who does the weaving: country weaves you, so that you become your ngurra (home) . Among Yolŋu, raki’ (string), twined from the bark fiber of the kurrajong tree in Wägilak ceremonial song from northeast Arnhem Land, stands for the connection between a present generation and its ancestors, and for the obligations and attachments that hold kin to one another .

A further dimension of the fold emerges in Indigenous critiques of colonial archives, where it can also mark sites of erasure, concealment, and woundedness. As Dana Claxton articulated at the Crossing Fonds symposium (), Indigenous knowledge often enters the archive not by invitation but appropriation, and the fold becomes a space where such knowledge is withheld in shadow. In her view, the fold carries the wounds of the archive, holding the dual potential for harm as well as for healing. Claxton’s vision complicates the aesthetics of inclusion by asking whether the archive’s folds can ever be complete without Indigenous presence, or whether they must remain in tension, stitched but never sealed.

Recognizing these genealogies reframes the fold from an elegant philosophical trope into a situated, relational ethic. Data never arrive as neutral sheets waiting to be pleated. Instead, power, custodianship, and vulnerability are already woven through them. A folding interface that expands an archive record while keeping provenance visible, or that leaves restricted materials enveloped unless proper ceremony is observed, honors this ethic.

div.head: Meanings
div.p: When weaving aspects of the fold into visual interfaces, four intertwined qualities can guide the design process: coherence, elasticity, infinity (), and depth.

Coherence requires that every partial view remains visibly tethered to the broader weave. Collapsing a family branch, filtering by period, or zooming out must leave the overall framework intact so that relations stay legible even when compressed. A collection interface should let readers open a facet without severing it from the fabric it rests on. A fold that erases its hidden layers breaks trust with both data and viewer.

Elasticity values supple transformation over brittle jumps. Interactive sliders, drag-to-weight controls, or touch-based stretch gestures should let the visual fabric give and rebound as interests evolve. Micro-animations that show nodes elongating before they settle or timelines bending under pressure make a change of view legible. Elasticity is a claim about interfaces, not on knowledge. Collections are full of discontinuities, in the form of destroyed, stolen, or withheld records. Applied indiscriminately, elasticity can smooth those gaps into a gradient. While a break that is an artifact of the current view can be animated, a break that belongs to the collection should stand out.

Infinity acknowledges that every unfolding is provisional. The word needs qualifying, since collections are indeed finite. What is open is the set of relations, not the holdings. Gradient fades at the canvas edge, or the refusal to display a triumphant ‘all items loaded’ badge, remind visitors that deeper pleats remain out of sight, sometimes because of cultural protocol, sometimes because the collection is simply unfinished. Better than a soft edge is a named one: this holding ends in this year because the donor’s papers do, or two hundred items are restricted and appear in no view. Stated that way, the exposed finitude is provenance information rather than a defect to be visually softened, while infinity conveys an ethic of humility.

Depth frames the fold as a layered space of memory. Every fold introduces a surface but also a recess, something set aside or held in reserve. This is not simply a matter of scale, but of responsibility: what lies beneath may be sacred or wounded. Designing with depth means acknowledging that not everything in a collection should be immediately seen, allowing space for latency and partiality. Visually, this can be signaled by shadow, blur, or layering. Depth unfolds in time, through gestures that require pause or reciprocal engagement before proceeding.

The fold offers a counterproposal to flattened dashboards and rigid result lists. Rather than pretending that data display is friction-free, it treats interaction as the skilled handling of cloth: stretching to reveal, relaxing to protect. Does a faceted filter sever a record from its custodial kin, or does it leave a visible selvedge of context? Akin to the idea of seamful visualizations exposing the stitches of their own making and the contingencies of the underlying data (), a folding interface earns trust not by hiding imperfections but by letting viewers sense where the weave is patched or worn thin.

div.head: Usage
div.p: The practical reach of folding has already been mapped in visualization research. A recent survey on un/foldable data visualizations () catalogs more than a hundred techniques that rely on progressive revealing and compressing rather than window-switching or pop-up layering. Across widely different data domains the survey demonstrates the same guiding logic: new detail is woven into the graphic surface while contextual cues remain present as scale shifts. Folds are not rare novelties but an emerging design pattern for visualizations of complex, stratified information. In the following, three collection interfaces illustrate the idea in distinct ways.

figure.head: Past Visions with the drawings filtered by the keyword Potsdam. Images that do not match fade and settle below the timeline, so the filtered selection stays legible against the whole collection rather than replacing it .

div.p: Past Visions is a dynamic visualization environment accommodating 1,492 nineteenth-century drawings by Frederick William IV of Prussia (1795-1861) on a zoomable and filterable canvas . The landing view positions every sheet—pertaining to a broad range of topics from urban planning to poetry—as a tiny thumbnail along a timeline whose granularity grows or shrinks as the viewer zooms into or out of the arrangement. The timeline features historical and biographical information contextualizing this collection. At the top of the interface is a linearized word cloud featuring subjects and themes characterizing the drawings. Filtering by theme gradually reshapes the arrangement of tags and images. The thumbnails not matching any selection criteria become translucent and gently move below the timeline (see Figure 2). Every state change is animated in place. In contrast to conventional interfaces, nothing jumps to a new window. At the maximum magnification the resolution is so high that it is possible to see the texture of pencil strokes and paper grain. Anonymous usage logs suggest that the gradually zoomable environment invites a rhythm of approach and retreat rather than a one-way drill-down.

From zooming to scrolling, Reading Traces visualizes Theodor Fontane’s (1819-1898) hand-library in a flexible form that can be gradually expanded and compressed via continuous scroll movements . The interface opens on a shelf-like band of 155 vertical bars, each bar a book; the varying widths of the bars encode how densely Fontane annotated that volume. Scrolling downward echoes running a finger along the spines: bars lengthen into page strips, and, with a further scroll, individual marginalia come out as colored squares that give access to facsimile scans. Scrolling in the opposite direction, the individual bars eventually merge into an overview summarizing the traces for each author. When the viewer shifts between different granularities, the bars and curves gradually stretch and compress without ever disappearing, allowing the eye to track continuity across scales. Resembling a complication in Deleuze’s terms, a toggle in the sidebar pivots the display into a similarity arrangement based on the character and frequency of marginalia left by Fontane for each author or book.

A different folding tactic guides Close-up Cloud, a visualization prototype built around the glass negatives by the photographer Wilhelm Weimar (1857-1917) at Hamburg’s Museum for Art and Design . Instead of presenting a synoptic overview first, as in the other cases, the interface begins as a graphical tag cloud featuring cropped details whose tile size reflects how often that motif occurs in the corpus. The tiles transition with a gentle cross-fading animation between different instances of the tag across the collection. Hovering over any tile reveals the tag’s name and frequency. Clicking on a tile centers the view and unfolds all the close-ups sharing this tag grouped by the respective glass negatives on which this tag has been placed. A second click on an item’s tile gently moves all the close-ups belonging to this negative to their exact coordinates on the original image, after which the full plate fades in, only then completing a full image of a glass negative.
Visitors can flip the entire display from negative to positive, converting the abstract originals into their more intuitive counterparts that better convey depth of the depicted artworks and design objects. The smooth transitions from fragmented detail views to cohesive object views illustrate how folding can invert the usual hierarchy of overview and detail: viewers begin immersed in minute fragments and only later assemble a coherent artifact, seeing the collection gradually unfold around the paths they take in the interface.

Coherence and elasticity are where these three are relatively strong, and depth is partly there: each stages the collection in layers and requires a descent to reach any single item. Its other half, the refusal to show, is untested since none of these collections holds restricted material. Infinity fares worst: a bounded, fully digitized corpus in each case, with no signal of what is missing.

div.head: Shimmer
div.p: Collection interfaces are more than scaffolds and surfaces. They can hold moments that feel alive, beckoning the visitor to pause and look closer. Such radiant moments are what can be called shimmer: a pulse of relational brilliance that discloses a hidden connection and suggests that a collection is a living ecology rather than a static repository. Shimmer is playful and unpredictable, and of the three terms discussed in this paper, it is the most speculative when it comes to the design of collection visualizations.

div.head: Origins
div.p:
The English word ‘shimmer’ refers to a wavering gleam, yet the concept is given far greater depth in the Yolŋu languages of northern Australia. There, bir’yun names the brilliance a surface acquires once it has been worked from dull to bright, a shimmer in which ancestral power is felt to be present . Just as a sudden break in a cloud can cause a river to flash, the finely cross-hatched lines of a painting can emit a similar radiance.
Deborah Bird Rose extends this concept to include multispecies lures: the blossom that attracts flying-fox pollinators, the patterns of song and dance that light up a ceremony, or the gleam of sunlight on wet leaves . Shimmer is therefore not a property held by any one thing but a capture running in several directions at once: water reflecting the sun, the sun glinting on the water, the eyes of the beholders caught and held. However, that vitality is precarious. Rose writes that extinction cascades drag shimmer from the world as relationships falter and species disappear . To notice shimmer is to sense both beauty and peril. When the term migrates into digital interfaces, the baggage comes with it. While the effect itself travels across cultures, its interpretation does not. A graphic that sparkles for mere effect resembles the stimulus, but drops everything that made it mean anything.

div.head: Meanings
div.p: Shimmer belongs to the family of what anthropologist Anna Tsing calls ‘arts of noticing’: practices that train perception to catch short-lived signals of entanglement before they slip away . In Yolŋu thought, bir’yun is a quality of the worked surface, and a painting need not even be seen for that quality to do its work: most ritual paintings are covered or rubbed out within hours, and much of the experience of them is a glimpse from the corner of the eye. The brilliance is relational in its meaning, which is culture-specific, while the experience of being captured by it reaches across cultures.

Ephemeral encounter. Translating shimmer to collection visualization demands that we reconceive graphical accent not as ornament but as a momentary co-presence between the aggregated collection and the wandering visitor. Because shimmer is inherently fleeting, it gestures toward a temporal ethics. It does not promise continuous access; instead, it models a shift in its appearance that respects ceremonial timing, ecological cycles, or community protocols. In design terms, this may mean valuing latency over permanence, making room for absence as an integral part of presence.

Precarious allure. Shimmer also carries the experience of fascination towards an entity that is at risk of destruction. The flash of vitality can slide into voyeuristic spectacle if severed from context, yet declining to lure at all risks rendering fragile ties invisible. The conceptual challenge is to hold allure in tension with responsibility: illumination must come twinned with an offer to reciprocate, through credit or stewardship.

Partial survival. The warning that extinction pulls shimmer from the world suggests that visualization should not cling to wholeness but acknowledge incompleteness. Brilliance indicates vitality, while its withdrawal registers loss. Rose distinguishes between dullness as a phase in a pulse, a resting state that can brighten again, and dullness as a flat absence. An interface that dims can mean either, and telling the two apart is the design problem: a collection between states looks much like one that is disappearing. A greyed-out facet may indicate a record under embargo, a digitization backlog, or a holding that no longer exists, and only the first of these will return. Shimmer therefore works as an invitation, calling attention to relations that need care if they are to persist.

Shimmer in a collection interface should therefore not be decorative sparkle but a carefully staged moment of lively, risky presence: it appears only long enough to allow a charge of curiosity and accountability, then dims so that other relations can come forward. Whether shimmer can be designed at all is doubtful. The effect is the tractable part, since brilliance is produced by technique and the light in a cross-hatched painting is real. What cannot be arranged is what a viewer brings to it, and it is there that the meaning of bir’yun stays with the source communities. A designer can only prepare conditions. This makes shimmer a term of reflection and interpretation more than of implementation or evaluation.

div.head: Usage
div.p: Although shimmer remains the most tentative of the three terms, some existing interfaces arrange conditions under which it might occur. None of the projects below was designed along the lines of shimmer, and none is offered here as proof that it was achieved. They can be read instead for possible rather than actual shimmers.

figure.head: The Marginalia Machine, a plotter that draws editorial notes onto a continuous paper scroll. A program separates the annotations from the underlying text as new documents from the Bloodaxe Archive are digitized, so the machine runs only while cataloguing is under way and stays silent between batches .

div.p: As part of the Poetics of the Archive project, the concept of archival liveness reimagines the digitization of the still-uncatalogued Bloodaxe Archive as a live event . A mechanical plotter slowly redraws handwritten notes from freshly scanned manuscripts on an endless paper scroll (see Figure 3), while a companion social media bot posts each fragment as it is being recognized. Because both systems operate only when new pages are being processed, the intermittent activity flares and subsides with the rhythms of the repository. Before the feed falls silent again, viewers may catch a glimpse of a poem title or a scrawled correction, reminding them that the collection is still becoming. Exposing the incompleteness of the catalog and the labor behind it also signals how easily this liveliness could be lost if the underlying work stalls.

The Speculative W@nderverse is not built for a canonical library, but for a private science fiction collection: 72 handmade anthologies compiled by Canadian superfan Bob Gibson. His cut-and-paste volumes mix forgotten pulp stories, comic panels, and marginalia . The interface treats this material as a living, unlikely cosmos. It features a keyword cloud and a hierarchy that form a hybrid taxonomy negotiating between fan keywords and scholarly terms. The covers of the anthologies are partially visible based on the current filters, and a timeline provides the temporal context of when the volumes were published. At the center of the hierarchy is a cluster of unfamiliar symbols that refer to themes, genres, and ratings, though a key for these symbols has not yet been found. When the cursor hovers over a symbol, the story’s cover art comes into focus, offering some clues as to what they might mean. These flashes of clarity are where I would locate shimmer’s precarious allure, provisionally, since the effect rests on a symbol key that has never been found. They reveal women authors absent from standard bibliographies and undated snippets of avant-la-lettre science fiction. By coupling fascination with the disclosure of absence, the interface transforms an idiosyncratic collection into a speculative laboratory where readers can glimpse the richness of science fiction’s great unread .

Lastly, the generative works Succession and Drifter remix large heritage datasets into endlessly recomposed visual ‘fossils’ . In Succession, five archival images linked to industrial Newcastle are superimposed in the browser, then slowly dissolve, making room for the next composite. Drifter harvests river-catchment maps, frog calls, and fragments from historic newspapers. Each refresh stitches a new alignment that lingers for only a minute before washing away. Viewers can save a fleeting arrangement, but the system returns immediately to its generative drift, underscoring that any captured frame is provisional. These projects stage conditions for shimmer as relational moments that may disclose entangled ‘matters of concern’ while refusing definitive closure. The brilliance here is produced by recombination, which yields it rarely.

What these three interfaces share is an openness to something that cannot be ensured. Any brilliance in them arrives, if it arrives at all, from a particular viewer meeting a unique arrangement in a specific situation. This makes shimmer the weakest of the three terms as a specification for design, yet a clear illustration of what vocabulary work can do. A concept that can neither be implemented nor measured still has the capacity to change what a diverse team may decide to leave room for.

div.head: A Grammar for Visual Collection Interfaces
div.p: At this point, the three terms are discrete entries in a small dictionary. A pidgin becomes useful only when words form phrases in acts of speech. The terms gain force when they are spoken in the situations where interfaces are imagined and interpreted: co-design workshops, community reviews, field deployments, and studio pedagogy. What follows outlines a grammar for visual collection interfaces. The principles formulate overarching commitments, a phrase book suggests how the terms can be combined, and a research framework proposes a methodology.

div.head: Principles
div.p: Wanderer, fold, and shimmer share more than a rhetorical affinity. Together they suggest a coherent way of thinking about interface design for collection visualizations.

Relationality. Conventional information systems treat data as self-contained objects waiting to be retrieved. The pidgin philosophy redirects attention to the ties that bind entities together and to the actors who forge and traverse those ties. The wanderer is defined not by arrival at a target but by a continuously renegotiated distance between self, record, and contexts. A collection is not a closed trove but a space for responsive accumulation: wanderers may annotate, trace paths, or offer commentary as participants in an expanding web of relations rather than as external observers. A fold does not add more content, but reorganizes adjacency and bends layers to center peripheral items. Shimmer puts the relational focus most sharply. The brilliance is produced by the surface, but what it comes to mean depends on what the viewer brings to the encounter. While it may seem romantic, shimmer points to a moment of affective tension in a situated encounter. In a collection interface built on the principle of relationality, the default unit of design is a connection: a co-citation, a shared provenance tag, or a kinship line.

Temporality. Standard usability doctrine values immediacy: pages that load in under two hundred milliseconds, search results that stream as you type. The pidgin philosophy argues instead for transitions that give temporal texture to the collection interface. The wanderer’s slow drift encourages hesitation and side-tracking, while the folds stretch or compress the movement between overview and detail, letting the eye acclimate. Shimmer offers an evanescent pulse that may or may not recur, reminding viewers that collections, like ecosystems, breathe. Designing with multiple tempos entails choreographing moments of stillness, such as a lingering hover before metadata blooms, alongside bursts of intensity. Attention to tempo counters the flattening effect of real-time dashboards, returning duration and rhythm to inquiry.

Partiality. The three terms also converge on an ethics of necessary incompleteness. Wandering accepts that some corridors remain closed; folds keep certain pleats latent to honor custodianship or cognitive load; shimmer appears only when conditions are right. Friction and refusal, often treated as obstacles to be engineered away, could become design affordances in their own right. This stance resonates with feminist critiques of full disclosure as a colonial gesture, Indigenous data-sovereignty protocols (), and growing privacy concerns . While archival policies increasingly accommodate such ethics, interface design has yet to catch up: few systems make partiality perceptible as part of the visitor experience. Interfaces that embrace partiality should therefore build in graceful dead-ends, consent-to-unfold gates, and quiet indicators that something is withheld.
Relationality, temporality, and partiality offer a compact set of principles for collection visualizations that foreground ties over nodes, rhythm over speed, and care over completeness.

div.head: Phrase book
div.p: The potential of this pidgin philosophy shows when people speak it at different stages along the life cycles of collection interfaces. Those situations include co-design workshops where sketches and collages prompt the generation and discussion of ideas, community reviews where ethical and technical tradeoffs are deliberated, field deployment when server logs and visitor feedback inform iterative refinement, and studio pedagogy where students test new terms against canonical vocabulary.

For these conversations, the three terms can assume complementary grammatical roles. The wanderer is the subject moving through digital information spaces. The fold provides the predicate embodying transformations of the visualizations during interaction. Finally, shimmer acts as an object that signals vitality and vulnerability. Constructions built from this trio serve as phrases that transdisciplinary groups can invoke while brainstorming, sketching, prototyping, testing, or teaching.

Wanderer → Fold. When an exploratory view brings a visitor to an unfamiliar node, whether a cloud of terms or a map of oral-history locations, the interface may allow the wanderer to fold the surrounding scene rather than open a modal window or redirect. The cloud contracts and the map reconfigures its layers, keeping peripheral traces visible while presenting focused detail. This construction can remedy dead-end navigation by offering a continuous transition that preserves orientation and respects the partiality of the larger context.

Fold + Shimmer. Here structural compression is punctuated by a transient element that signals depth. After a branch in a hierarchy or an interval in a timeline is folded, the newly condensed element can carry a brief emphasis, such as a visual pulse of light, scaled to the density or sensitivity of the material now tucked away. Whether that emphasis registers as shimmer is not up to the designer, but if it does, it marks that the relations are still there and tells the visitor where to look for them.

Wanderer ↔ Shimmer. In this phrase, the agency of the terms may alternate as the shimmer invites the wanderer’s attention, who in turn might seek to find shimmer. During periods of tentative hovering, common in image, sound, or mixed-media collections, a restrained emphasis may appear on an adjacent yet unexplored record. If the visitor accepts the invitation, the path branches sideways, and control then returns to the visitor. The interplay balances guided discovery with exploratory autonomy, which distinguishes it from a conventional recommendation cue.

Wanderer → Fold → Shimmer. Lastly, the tripartite phrase articulates complex information experiences. Lateral wandering establishes the scope of what is there, folding reveals how it is layered, and a brief emphasis on a single element can open up the experience of shimmer. The pattern could be applied across a range of domains, from literary corpora to biodiversity databases, giving each collection a sequence for working out what relationality, temporality, and partiality mean in its own case. What counts as a lateral move differs between a set of letters and a set of species records, as does what should be foldable and what deserves a moment of emphasis.

These phrases are not tried and tested templates to be copied wholesale. Like clauses in any living language, they invite elaboration, inversion, or abandonment as local constraints and ambitions dictate.

div.head: Research framework
div.p: Because the grammar of the pidgin philosophy claims fidelity to design practice as much as to interpretive scholarship, its research program should combine methods drawn from those traditions. I organize them into three overlapping passes that can repeat and inform each other in any order: designerly probing, humanistic reading, and situated evaluation.

Designerly probing treats visualization creation as a research process in its own right. Here the team works through iterative sandcastles () that follow one emerging question at a time: a constellation view that foregrounds wandering, or an elastic stack that resembles folding. Situated cultural-probe exercises, such as sketchbooks or speculative postcards, can prompt participants to voice sensory memories and contested readings of a place, demonstrating how in-situ design probes stimulate plural, critical perspectives on cultural heritage . Collaborative critique sessions borrow from reflective practice: collages are pinned up and openly discussed in the group to inform the next iteration . The outcome is not a finished product but a clarified design question.

Humanistic reading replays prototype sessions as if they were texts: screen recordings and transcriptions of think-aloud expressions become trace documents for close reading and thick description. Rather than asking whether a visitor completed a task, the reading asks what a pause was doing, where an expectation was disappointed, and which vocabulary a participant reached for when the interface offered none. Collaborators should pursue their own readings of prototypes to formulate ‘friendly critique’ and give suggestions for iterations. Indigenous elders may refuse a fold that exposes restricted knowledge, while poets may celebrate a wandering path that produces serendipitous juxtapositions. These hermeneutic moves return ethical and cultural nuance to what could otherwise remain purely interactional data.

Situated evaluation investigates how the pidgin philosophy holds up in real encounters with an interface. However, the canonical metrics tend to capture the wrong thing. Dwell time, click depth, and task completion may measure efficiency, but a wanderer who lingers is indistinguishable from a visitor who has left the room. Logs can be useful, but as traces to be read rather than aggregated. A single session replayed as a path shows where a visitor doubled back, which unfolding was abandoned midway, and when a threshold was never crossed. In addition to these, observations and interviews with visitors, curators, archivists, and community members can determine if the terms represent anything meaningful in their encounters with the collection.

The three passes circulate in a spiral. A puzzling pattern in the traces may send designers back to build another prototype, while a close reading of a fold that participants consistently misread suggests a different kind of vocabulary. Design iterations produce new material for interpretation. Throughout, the open glossary serves as a kind of knowledge base: heuristics are tagged with observations, terms fork into stricter or looser dialects, and new words enter when existing ones no longer speak to an emerging practice. Each strand honors relationality through collaboration across expertise, temporality through an iterative rhythm rather than a waterfall, and partiality through the admission that no single method can claim total truth.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: This pidgin philosophy sets out a vocabulary and grammar for the design and study of data visualizations of archival fonds and cultural collections, yet several important aspects fall outside the scope of this paper. Below I briefly acknowledge key concerns that are readable as shortcomings of the framework or as directions for future work.

Infrastructural debt. Behind every elegant interface lies a hidden accrual of technical and organizational liabilities. Digitization backlogs often delay whole swaths of a collection, while grant cycles dictate which servers are maintained and which silently age. Cold-storage cloud tiers can make a master file effectively unreachable just when a community demands higher-resolution evidence. As the Endings Project has shown, most cultural-heritage sites are launched with short-term funds but without a plan to migrate code, refresh formats, or document bespoke stacks once the grant ends. The result is a maintenance burden that outstrips staff capacity and makes even the most ethically charged shimmer meaningless the moment the underlying asset decays or the framework breaks after a security update . To keep the pidgin realistic, any grammar of interfaces needs an underlying lexicon that names the conditions for preservation. Making the terms of maintenance explicit in early scoping meetings would let collaborators weigh visual ambition against long-term resilience.

Data-capture politics. In this paper, I consider collections as given, yet many digital archives originate in contexts of injustice ranging from colonial extraction to surveillance regimes . The principle of partiality, with its license to blur, hide, or withhold, mitigates some downstream harm, but it cannot undo the coercive conditions under which some of these records were first ‘captured.’ To confront that history the lexicon itself needs new terms. A consent ledger could travel with a record, logging who authorized what use and when that consent expires. A refusal register would document requests by source communities to suppress, restrict, or repatriate items; a sovereignty tag might mark materials governed by Indigenous data protocols such as CARE . Embedding such terms, along with the accompanying technical specifications, would extend the pidgin from design for encounter to the conditions of capture, and open a path to restitution or deletion where justice demands it. However, what constitutes justice or violence depends on the specific situation. The same act may be perceived as preservation in one community and as a violation in another. Navigating these tensions requires a language that enables dialogue across value systems shaped by time and place.

Risk of oversimplification. Any pidgin gains its usefulness by limiting language to negotiable chunks. Rendering wanderer, fold, and shimmer as design heuristics inevitably compresses the dense strata of philosophies from which they spring. What begins as a mobile metaphor can become a decorative trope, an instruction to add a shimmer effect here and insert a fold there, detached from the histories the terms were meant to foreground. The pidgin’s brevity is a provisional bridge, not a destination. Each term should act as a prompt to return to its source traditions, to cite them, and to involve their living communities where possible. The pidgin itself must remain seamful (): its visible stitches should remind designers that behind every concise phrase lies a thicker fabric of theory and practice that must be revisited if the critical force of the concepts is not to fray.

Ocular-centrism. This project assumes that knowledge is encountered first and foremost through the eye: a wanderer glances across a visual field, folds reshape a graphic surface, and shimmer flashes as transient light. Such emphasis risks marginalizing collections whose primary materials are sonic or haptic, and it under-serves communities that approach collections through touch, voice, or vibration. Extending the pidgin therefore means recruiting new parts of speech. A term like ‘echo’ might designate a reverberant relation that emerges only when sounds overlap in time. Similarly, ‘grain’ could name the tactile residue that lingers after a page is handled. Developing such multisensory terms, and pairing them with interface techniques that privilege hearing or touch, would counter the bias toward sight and offer more inclusive grammars for collections whose stories should resonate beyond the visual.

Distance from archival practice. Admittedly, the conversation described here barely touches the daily work of description, delivery, and discovery. The people who write finding aids and answer reference queries are rarely involved when a collection interface is designed, and their perspectives may differ from the ones assumed above. Slowness, there, is not an ethic but a service failure. A term is only useful for a practitioner if it links to something already in their frame of reference. Fold fits in readily, since a finding aid is itself a folded structure, and most discovery interfaces render it badly. Wanderer fits since it suggests a kind of browsing that reference statistics have never recorded and failed to support. Shimmer attaches to nothing I can identify at this point. If this pidgin philosophy is to travel, the intention is not to simply propagate three words but to learn how they resonate with, and rub against, archival practices.

Asymmetry in the metaphor. A pidgin is not a meeting of equals. Its lexicon comes primarily from one of the languages in contact, while its grammar comes primarily from none of them . Something is always supplying the words, and it is rarely the party with the least power, even if the direction of dominance is not uniform. Likewise, the settings described in this paper are not level either. Design and software vocabulary tends to set the terms, since it is attached to what will actually get built, while archivists and humanities scholars more often do the translating. This paper is not exempt, since some of the terms are in part borrowed from Indigenous thought, from communities who were not included when the borrowing happened. Naming a lexicon is itself an act of authority, and a pidgin philosophy that only celebrates hybridity would miss this. The more demanding question is not what the words mean but who gets to coin them, and whether the people who hold the material can shape a prototype as forcefully as the people who build it.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper set out to do three things. The first was to trace the emergence of a pidgin philosophy in the trading zone of archival studies, interface design, and the digital humanities, and to argue for vocabulary work as a methodological stance. The second was to describe three terms, wanderer, fold, and shimmer, through their lineages, theoretical commitments, and practical uses. The third was to synthesize them into a grammar: the principles of relationality, temporality, and partiality, a phrase book for combining the terms, and a tripartite research framework.

I opened with a workshop that was never meant to produce an interface. The aim was to stimulate a mixed group’s imagination about what a photo archive might become on screen, and to test a format for prompting that kind of conversation . What the afternoon produced was a group who could, for a few hours, discuss the same collection in the same words. That idiom did not outlive the day, and no single interface can be traced to it. What travelled was the format: collaging proved a durable way of bringing people with different expertise into a common language, and it carried into more than a decade of visualization projects in Potsdam . The conversation itself likely informed Amber’s later redevelopment of its own website, and echoes of it persist in the terms gathered here. The afterlife was largely methodological. That is what this paper has been trying to name.

The lexicon and its grammar suggest how vocabulary work might function as a methodological resource for design and research. Considering visitors as wanderers foregrounds surprise and slowness and makes room for lingering. Modeling interaction as folding keeps continuity and tension as qualities worth designing for. Letting shimmer appear and recede directs attention to the vitality and vulnerability of cultural collections and to the care they require. Whether these terms do such work beyond the settings in which I have used them remains an open question, and the research framework sketches one way of finding out.

Any pidgin remains provisional. A contact language stays alive by being spoken, revised, and contested. The lexicon presented here is therefore an opening rather than a closure. Future collaborations will need new terms that speak, for example, to sound archives or haptic collections and will uncover contexts in which these three fail to evoke interest or imagination. Fresh words can be coined, old ones retired, and familiar phrases adjusted to fit local ethics and aesthetics. Which words those turn out to be, and who gets to propose them, will be settled in the collaborations themselves rather than in a paper.
